title_en: Rings of Power Showrunner Explains the ‘Different Side’ of Simon Pegg’s Balrog: It ‘Actually Is True to the Books’
summary_en: The Rings of Power Season 3 is full of creatures and bigger canon references, from Simon Pegg's Balrog to the Fell Beasts, Oliphaunts, Great Eagles and more.
body_en:
Spoilers follow for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3, Episodes 1-8.
The third season of Prime Video’s The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has come to a close, strengthening its ties to author J.R.R. Tolkien's mythology, creatures and iconography, and even explicitly leaning into the design and execution of creatures and places seen in Peter Jackson’s film adaptation. If you’re not a canon expert a la Stephen Colbert, or haven’t re-watched the films recently, below is an explainer on many of the creatures featured in Season 3, with insight into how they connect to the books or the films.
Balrogs were servants of Morgoth, the Dark Lord, during the First Age. After his fall from power, many Balrogs were wiped out in battle, but a few survived. In The Rings of Power narrative, at least one lived deep inside the Misty Mountains, and it was awakened by the dwarves mining for Mithril.
In "Orodruin,” Sauron seeks out that particular Balrog (voiced by Simon Pegg) to gain its knowledge about safely using the Flame of Udûn to forge the One Ring. In return, Sauron promises to free the creature and give it Khazad-dûm to rule. Co-showrunner Patrick McKay told IGN that Tolkien’s text describing the Balrog influenced how they interpreted the fire beast.
“One of the things that's cool in the books is if you really look into the lore that Tolkien built for his entire life, the Balrogs are intelligent super-beings,” McKay explained. “They aren't just monsters. They're cunning and they are battlefield commanders in the First Age. It opened up the possibility that we could show you a different side of him. Maybe one you're not expecting, but one that actually is true to the books and the conception.”
McKay and Episode 7 director Stefan Schwartz described the scene in the Misty Mountains as a dramatic “negotiation” between the Balrog and Sauron. “The scene goes from [Balrog’s] total disdain to actually being won over by Sauron to actually helping him in his quest to create this ring,” Schwartz pointed out.
McKay said casting director Theo Park came up with the idea of asking Simon Pegg to voice the Balrog opposite Charlie Vickers’ Sauron. “Simon Pegg is often known as a comedic actor because of the earliest films he did with Edgar Wright, but he can kind of do anything,” McKay said. “This was an opportunity to do something he hadn't done before, and he took to it like a duck to water.”
Schwartz confirmed that Pegg was on set, performing live into a microphone to Vickers, who was looking at a light box which represented the Balrog’s placement in the frame. “They could rehearse it and run the lines and then actually play it, and then we could talk about the nuance of how he is brought over to Sauron's way of thinking,” he said.
An ally of Sauron’s by the end of Season 3, the Balrog’s rule over King Thrain (Eddie Marsan) and the dwarves will play out in Season 4 (and 5 if it gets a greenlight).
In the opening minutes of Episode 4, "Gundabad," Sauron is introduced to his future steed — an extremely ornery beast that is resistant to the bridle. In Tolkien’s letters, the author described them as winged, stinking creatures with no feathers, just bare skin. The author also referred to them as fell beasts, as well as Nazgûl-birds, which makes sense because in the book version of The Return of the King, fell beasts become the replacement steeds for the Ringwraiths.
However in The Rings of Power, Sauron expounds on their origins more specifically, telling the orcs, “They were once eagles, you know. Until Morgoth blessed them with his touch. Taught them to crave his lash, to survive on only the foulest of meats.” Because of that, Sauron knows the way to tame one is through feeding it living flesh, which he does by feeding it random orcs. The steady meals allow Sauron to bridle the beast, which he first uses to chase Galadriel to Mount Gundabad and then the forests of Greenwood. By the end of the season, Sauron has taught Nazgnagôl Theo ( Tyroe Muhafidin ), and likely the others, how to ride a fell beast. He uses it to dive-bomb the Númenórean army and freak out their soldiers on the eve of battle. Look for them to return when the real war between Sauron and Middle-earth begins in a future season.
In the last minutes of "Gundabad," before Galadriel, Arondir, Celeborn and Marnûkh are trapped by Sauron and Nazgnagôl Theo on a ledge in Mount Gundabad, Galadriel releases a flaming arrow into the sky like a rescue flare. It spurs a snow-covered Giant Eagle in the mountain to awaken and fly into action. Galadriel instantly recognizes it is Landroval, Prince of Eagles. He gets hit by an orc arrow but survives to save Galadriel and Celeborn from falling to their deaths.
Landroval is a heroic figure across Tolkien’s ages. In The Hobbit, the eagle will save Thorin and company from the burning trees. And at the end of The Return of the King, Landroval is one of the three Great Eagles who rescue Frodo Baggins and Samwise Gamgee from Mordor after they destroy the One Ring.
The elephant-like creatures found south of Mordor are called oliphaunts in Tolkien’s text, and are formally introduced in The Rings of Power in Episode 3, "The Secret Fire.” Gandalf comes upon one in battle armor under the Dark Magic control of Pallando (Ciarán Hinds). Despite getting thrown around by the aggravated beast, Gandalf frees the creature from its constraints in an act of kindness. In "The Lady of Lórien," Gandalf tries to turn Pallando away from Sauron but gets knocked out by the Dark Wizard and is instead bound and strung up to ride prone, on top of an oliphaunt, as he’s taken to Sauron.
In Peter Jackson’s The Two Towers, oliphaunts are visually established in live-action battles, though they are entirely CGI creations. Showrunners Patrick McKay and J. D. Payne decided to carry through that take on the creature into The Rings of Power for continuity.
In Episode 3, "The Secret Fire,” Gandalf has a vision when he visits the Secret Fire and realizes his mission is to redeem Pallando, not conquer him. When he returns to Tom Bombadil’s cottage, his friend is gone and all that’s left is his signature hat. Gandalf takes it as his own, completing the iconic silhouette — long beard, staff and hat — that’s synonymous with the wizard.
In the finale, "The Doom of Men,” Gandalf crosses paths with Tom once again on his long journey back to the elves. His wizarding mentor tells him to keep the hat, cementing its new ownership with his blessing.
What creatures or references did you pick up on in Rings of Power Season 3? Let’s discuss in the comments!
